content.thinking:
I'm planning the design for a whimsical barnstormer biplane, basing proportions on real planes like the Waco or Stearman but exaggerating the fuselage, cowling, and propeller for a cheerful, cartoonish feel, and I want to write the whole module carefully in one pass to avoid needing to debug.

I'm now sketching the rig itself: the fuselage as the root, with hinge joints for the propeller, wheels, rudder, elevators, and ailerons, making sure each part is explicitly bound to its bone to avoid relying on fragile defaults. I'm setting up a consistent helper pattern so every part always passes its bone explicitly, then starting to define the joint list beginning with the fuselage root position.

Adding the four aileron hinges plus a tail wheel skid joint, pilot head, and a whimsical scarf tail built as a chain of three joints swept into a flattened ribbon shape.

Pilot can be a simple torso/head capsule with leather cap, goggles, and scarf, keeping only head and scarf as jointed. Wing struts stay static, but I could add a small whimsical touch like a pennant flag hinged on the upper wing strut, maybe with bunting between wings for extra charm.

For the bunting, I'm thinking triangle flags along a curved path between strut tips, using card geometry with SVG pennant textures in multiple colors, bound to the body bone so they move correctly. For sizing, I'll go with a chubby whimsical biplane proportion -- roughly 9m upper wingspan, 8m lower, 7m fuselage length, with an exaggerated round cowl for charm.

Now I'm working out the vertical layout: wheel radius 0.5 sets the ground clearance, fuselage centered around y=1.55 with the lower wing mounted near the belly and the upper wing suspended via cabane struts about 1.4m above, giving a proper biplane gap. For the longitudinal (Z) placement along the nose, I'm positioning the prop spinner, cowling, and planning to use a lathe revolve around the fuselage axis to shape the rounded cowl.

Still building fuselage geometry... I'm lofting the body from the cowling station back to a tapered tail tip, defining elliptical cross-sections at each station and orienting the sweep frames so the tube follows the nose-to-tail path with proper vertical and horizontal proportions for a tubby, rounded teardrop shape.

For the cockpit I'm planning an open cutout: a dark recessed disc with a padded coaming rim, housing a pilot figure and possibly a second passenger seat further aft, matching a barnstormer-style layout.

Adding cockpit coaming rim geometry...

Working out the scale factors so the tube thickness scales proportionally with the torus, then checking how the rim height compares to the curved fuselage surface at different x positions near the top.

I realize the rim would float above the surface by about 0.12 at the edges since the fuselage curves down faster than the flat ring. I'm reconsidering the cockpit as a raised coaming instead—something with sloped sides that meet the surface, maybe using a scaled cylinder geometry.

Trying another approach: a small bowl-shaped ellipsoid sunk into the fuselage, but that risks creating a bulge rather than a true hole. I think the cleanest fix is a proper cockpit coaming built from an elliptical cylinder, scaled down and positioned so its sides blend into the fuselage surface.

Working out the geometry, the coaming's bottom edge just reaches the fuselage skin, with its top rim above that — then I'll add a thin dark disc tucked just inside the rim to fake the depth of an open cockpit, plus a torus ring at the rim itself in a contrasting trim color so it reads as a real opening rather than a bump. The coaming walls stay in leather brown, the disc stays dark, and the pilot figure will sit inside this recessed area.

For the pilot, I'm building a torso capsule rising out of the disc and a head above it — overlap with the disc is fine since the body breaks up the silhouette anyway.

Now for the wings, I'm working out how to extrude a wing shape from a flat plan-view outline, figuring out the right coordinate axes for span, chord, and thickness so the extrusion direction lines up correctly and the wing sits flat with rounded, whimsical tips rather than sharp ones.

Still refining wing geometry... thinking through a pillowy tapered profile with bevels, painted rib stripes running chordwise, darker leading-edge bands, red wingtip accents, and separate aileron cutouts at the trailing edge.

I'll avoid rounded corners that risk self-crossing, instead building the rounded tip explicitly with arc points, and define the wing chord coordinates with forward edge at +c/2 and rear at -c/2.

Working out the elliptical tip geometry with sample angles, then listing the full outline points going front to tip to rear...

Mapping out the aileron notch position along the trailing edge, keeping it within the straight section before the tip rounding begins.

I'm tracing the outline ordering clockwise, mapping the front edge, right tip arc, and notch transition points to make sure the aileron slit aligns correctly with the main wing geometry.

Now I'm working out the rear edge and the left tip arc coordinates symmetrically, parameterizing each tip's angle sweep (rear-to-front for the left side, front-to-rear for the right) so the two arcs mirror each other properly in the outline.

I'm checking the full polygon closes correctly without duplicate points, keeping orientation consistent around the shape, then figuring out the notch spacing before moving to the aileron rectangle coordinates.

Defining aileron geometry...

Working out the thickness axis, then setting main wing thickness thicker than the aileron for visual hierarchy. I'm planning a paint function that distinguishes top and bottom wing surfaces based on normal direction, using fabric-like coloring with panel lines and rib details.

I'm leaning toward a cheerful, whimsical palette with warm-top/cool-bottom shading rather than pulling in toon or glow kits — simpler custom paints should carry the mood fine without extra dependencies. Now I'm moving on to planning the interplane struts, placing paired supports on each side of the fuselage.

Writing strut geometry...

Now I need thin bracing wires in an X pattern between struts, plus cabane struts connecting the fuselage top near the cockpit to the upper wing center, working out the exact attachment coordinates for each.

I'm checking proportions against the real Stearman for reference, but realize the pilot's head position would collide with the upper wing at current heights, so I need to raise the upper wing and rescale the overall fuselage height to keep things proportional while staying intentionally a bit tubbier and whimsical than the real aircraft.

I'm sizing chunky balloon tires at radius 0.5 with axle height 0.5, checking that the short landing gear struts give enough ground clearance, since the propeller needs room to spin without hitting the ground.

Settling on fuselage centered at y=1.4 so the prop clears the ground with margin, which pushes the wing to y=3.05 and adjusts strut length to about 0.5.

For landing gear, I'm placing wheels at x=±0.95, z=0.75, connected via splayed V-struts from the fuselage down to the axles, with a thin axle rod spanning across between the wheels to tie the gear together visually.

Each wheel hub uses a chunky torus for the tire with its axis rotated to align along X, plus a cylinder disc for the hub, and I'm considering adding a simple spoke or star decal texture on the hub face for detail.

I'll skip wheel spats since those belong on the body, not the wheel itself, and now I'm figuring out placement for a small tail wheel positioned under the rear fuselage.

Since the fuselage sits level rather than in a tail-down stance, a long tail skid leg would look odd, so instead I'll give the tail a slight upward stylized curve toward the fin tip for a whimsical upswept look.

I'm sizing a small curved tail skid — a swept tube running from the fuselage underside down to a tiny wheel, keeping the rear fuselage profile low and tapered toward the tail.

For the horizontal stabilizer and elevators, I'm planning to reuse the same plan-outline generator used for the wings, defining a shared function that produces the main surface shape plus a notched elevator/aileron cutout so it can be reused across upper wing, lower wing, and tail surfaces.

For the fin and rudder, I'm switching to a vertical extrusion orientation where the outline runs along forward-Z and up-Y, placing the fin at the fuselage reference point and sketching its rounded leading-edge shape as a series of absolute coordinate points.

Fixing the fin outline with the hinge at z=-3.52, making sure the base sits properly inside the fuselage radius at that point, then setting up the rudder's joint and outline relative to the hinge.

The winding direction doesn't matter much. I'm figuring out part placement relative to bone ownership — the rudder rides the rudder bone, the stabilizer sits at a fixed fuselage position, and the elevator hinges there too. Now I'm sketching the propeller as a two-blade wooden shape, outlining its blade profile in the front view plane.

Finishing the lower half mirrors the shape into a symmetric narrow-waisted blade with a slight twist, giving it a thin extruded depth and beveled edges plus a slight tilt to feel "at rest."

I'm painting the propeller with a wood-grain base and yellow tip bands near the outer edges, then thinking about a rounded dome-shaped spinner lathed around the hub axis to give a whimsical nose cone look.

Now I'm positioning the spinner at the hub and sketching a cowling profile lathed around the z-axis with a bulging lip shape to wrap the front of the engine housing.

Placing the cylinder heads...

I'm working out the cowl's front face paint using position-based shading—darker near the engine plate center with a ring highlight, keeping the lathe profile with the lip pinch near the front edge simple.

Now I'm settling on a whimsical barnstormer palette: cherry red body with cream countershaded belly, teal accent band, yellow highlights, navy, brown leather, and metal tones, all kept under 64 flat colors. I'm writing the fuselage paint function with a red-top/cream-belly split at a fixed height, plus a wavy teal stripe along the side based on position.

I'm also planning a big "7" roundel decal on each side of the fuselage using SVG decals projected onto the sweep surface, making sure the orientation faces outward on both left and right flanks so the text reads correctly from either side.

Working through the vector math to confirm each side's viewing direction keeps the number upright and nose-to-tail readable rather than mirrored.

Since symmetric roundel designs don't care about mirroring, I'll skip flipping either side and just place decals directly on the fuselage surface, using a planar texture approach for wing roundels as well.

Working through the orientation math for top vs. bottom wing decals...

I'm thinking about adding roundel decals to the wing tops and bottoms, plus some lettering like a tail banner or fuselage text—keeping font use minimal and generic since rendering support is uncertain, maybe a number inside a roundel instead of risky text.

For the pilot, I'm picturing a chubby whimsical aviator built from simple parts: a capsule body in a brown leather jacket, a sphere head with skin tone, a leather cap with flaps, goggles made of brass-rimmed spheres with teal lenses, and small added features like a nose sphere and mustache pieces to give the face some character.

Working out the cap flaps, chin strap, and pilot scarf details, then planning the fuselage station coordinates to position the head and cockpit correctly along the body.

Working out the coaming geometry so the rim meets the surface properly, I'm computing the front cockpit coaming as a cylinder with rim top around 2.12 and a torus detail at the lip, then setting up the rear cockpit coaming similarly with its top near 2.0.

For passengers, I'm placing a teddy bear in the front cockpit built from spheres for body and head plus ears, muzzle, bow tie, and tiny aviator goggles, checking it clears the upper wing underside comfortably. In the rear cockpit I'm adding a pilot figure using a capsule torso and spherical head with a cap, confirming clearance under the wing too, then thinking through how to add small tilted windscreens in front of each cockpit using a thin extruded frame shape in light blue with brass trim.

Making the frame outline slightly larger than the glass so a visible rim shows around and in front, then planning to build a reusable windscreen helper function for both the front and rear canopy pieces on the Stearman.

Now I'm positioning the cabane struts connecting the fuselage to the upper wing center-section, checking that the front struts clear the nose cowl and the rear struts avoid colliding with the rear cockpit coaming by widening their attachment points along the fuselage.

I'm now working on the interplane struts further outboard, placing front and rear strut pairs between the lower and upper wings while accounting for the stagger between them.

Working out the diagonal bracing wires connecting the lower wing roots to the strut tops and the cabane struts, computing the coordinate pairs for each bay.

I'll add diagonal drag wires crossing between the front and rear struts in the side plane, skipping tiny fitting spheres at the ends to keep things simple, then move on to wing leading edge details.

For wing surface coloring, I'm defining paint logic along the span and chord: a leading-edge band near the front, red tip markers with white bands near the wingtips, thin dark rib-stitch lines spaced along the chord, plus subtle shading, with the aileron painted red.

Writing wing paint function...

Adding more rib and shading details...

Thinking about fun extras like a bear passenger, then adding exhaust pipe stubs curving back from the cowl sides and a turtledeck fairing behind the rear cockpit.

I'm figuring out a small headrest bump positioned on the fuselage top with a scaled sphere so it sits just above the surface. I'm also considering a tiny pitot tube rod on the strut, skipping a compass detail, and thinking about whether to add a subtle glow to the pilot's goggles or a nose lamp.

Now I'm adding navigation lights using a glow kit — red on the left wingtip and green on the right, placed as small protruding spheres near the tip edges of the upper wing. I'm also thinking about a small decorative fuel cap cylinder on the upper wing center, skipping a walking surface detail, and considering thin torus rings around the fuselage to suggest panel seams.

I'm working out paint patterns: fabric-skinning seam lines running vertically along the body using a periodic darker maroon tone, plus a sunburst-style cowl paint scheme with concentric teal and cream bands near the engine cowl lip, determined by z-position bands.

Now I'm color-coding the rest of the plane: red body, cream wings with red tips, teal tail surfaces, and a striped barnstormer rudder alternating red, cream, and teal bands. I'm also figuring out orientation math so a star decal painted on the fin reads correctly mirrored depending on which side faces the viewer.

I'll skip the idea of giving the cowl a cartoon smiley face since the pilot and bear already give the plane plenty of character, and instead add decorative bunting strung between the wingtips, strut tops, and cabane struts as a playful finishing touch.

Maybe simpler: string bunting between the two front struts at mid-height, spanning left to right in front of the fuselage, letting it droop slightly across the cockpit area.

Actually simpler: skip wingtip bunting and instead add a small pennant flag on a pole mounted atop the fin, placing the pole base near the fin top around height 2.65 extending up to about 3.05, with the pennant extruding backward.

I'm positioning the pole along the fin's trailing edge, placing it between the top and bottom bounds with the pennant attached near the top. Now I'm starting to define the skeleton joints for the structure.

For the body, I'm setting a root joint without a specific role, then giving the propeller and main wheels hinge roles. For the tail wheel, I'm considering splitting it into a swivel joint for steering and a separate hinge for the axle rotation, with the fork and wheel parts distributed between them, then continuing with hinge roles for the rudder and elevator surfaces.

Now I'm adding ailerons as hinge joints, treating the wing flaps similarly as lid-like hinges. I'm also planning a pilot head joint using the "head" role, a scarf as a three-joint tail chain, and a pennant hinge, bringing the total joint count to roughly twenty, which seems reasonable. I'm also thinking through how positions and parent relationships for these hinge joints should be specified.

For the scarf chain, I'm setting up a curved path with four points that stream back and up to suggest a wave, using default chain naming so the segments become scarf1 through scarf3. Then I'm planning the sweep geometry for the tubes, using a box-shaped cross section with a radius function that tapers along the chain to give it a tapered, fringed look.

I'm working through the ribbon's color bands (yellow fading to red at the tip) and the orientation logic, deciding whether to set an `up` axis so the flat ribbon face flutters vertically like a real scarf rather than lying flat horizontally.

Good enough either way, so I'll move forward with that choice. I need to keep triangle counts under budget by using low segment counts on spheres, then start writing the implementation with the necessary imports and types.

Setting up imports and helpers...

I'm now defining the builder function with joints for the body, propeller, and wheels, setting positions and hinge directions for each part. I'm checking whether the mirrored wheel joint direction could cause any symmetry issues.

I'm sketching out the tail wheel swivel and its child wheel joint, then moving on to define aileron hinge parameters and the geometry constants for the upper wing, lower wing, and tail stabilizer — span, chord, taper ratio, and sweep offsets for each surface.

Lowering the lower wing to y=1.25 so it tucks against the fuselage belly, checking clearance against the fuselage's bottom and center height. Now I'm writing a plan function that builds the outline points for each wing surface from these parameters, computing root/tip chord positions and hinge line locations.

Writing outline generator function...

Still defining flap geometry and extrusion logic...

I also want to add small surface details like ribs, nav lights, and roundels, plus a separate flap-extrusion step with its own thickness and bevel. Then I'll define a wing paint helper that returns color strings from a shared palette for top and bottom surfaces with accent options.

Writing wing paint shader...

Decided ailerons get teal fabric with cream ribs for contrast, plus spanwise stripes on top for visual interest. Now I'm shaping the cowl using a lathe profile, defining the radius curve along the axis and double-checking how the axis distances translate to the y-parameter at each point.

Checking how the cowl profile radii compare to the fuselage station radii near z=2.1–2.35, since the cowl needs to blend smoothly into the fuselage's rounded nose cap rather than creating a step or gap.

For the cowl paint logic, I'm deciding to model it as a hollow shell with separate outer and inner wall radii rather than a solid cone, so the engine face reads as recessed inside an open cowling. Writing the shell profile coordinates...

I'll skip smoothing and keep a sharp low-poly polyline with 14 segments, accepting faceted creases where corners exceed 35°. For the engine, I'm placing a dark cylinder as the crankcase along the z-axis with cylinder heads arranged radially, protruding slightly past the front lip.

Rather than hiding the radial engine behind the cowl, I'll expose stubby finned cylinder heads pointing forward at the face, sized small enough to fit within the cowl lip's inner radius, with a dark cylindrical core and a front cap disc.

I'm figuring out the crank hub connecting the engine face to the spinner, then working out the spinner's lathe profile so the propeller blades pass through it cleanly at the hub, tapering from a wide base down to the tip.

For materials, I'm thinking wood tones for the prop and a shiny brass-yellow for the spinner. Now I'm sketching out the fuselage loft itself, setting up stations with position, width, and height, and using the default octagonal sweep for the cross-section.

Actually I want softer, rounder shapes, so I'll bump the sweep to 12 sides instead. For the color palette, I'm landing on a red fuselage, a butter-yellow cowl, cream wings with red leading edges and teal ailerons, and teal/red tail stripes -- a deliberately clashing but playful whimsical look.

I'm also deciding on brown leather interior, brass spinner, navy landing gear struts, and dark navy tires with cream sidewalls and hubs. For the body shading, I'm setting up a cel-shaded paint logic using surface normals -- brighter red on top-facing surfaces, darker red shadow below, cream on the belly, and a teal stripe band along the fuselage side, adjusting for how the tail's centerline shifts.

Working out stripe curve math...

I'm making the banding run continuously along the surface regardless of normal direction, so the teal band tapers smoothly at the tail tip without leaving gaps. I'll add dark seam lines at regular z-intervals, and consider adding a ring of rivets around the cowl rim for extra detail.

Positioning rivets around the cowl lip and sizing small spheres to sit flush against the brass surface, then sketching exhaust stack pipes that sweep from the engine housing down the side of the fuselage with tapering radius and rounded caps.

Working out the gear struts geometry... I'm positioning the wheel at x=1.0 with faired struts connecting front and rear legs down to the axle points near the fuselage.

I'm checking fuselage curvature at x=0.35 to confirm the leg start points sit just outside the body surface, then placing a dark metal axle rod connecting both sides beneath the fuselage, skipping extra shock-collar details for simplicity.

For the tail skid I'm defining a curved leg path down to a swivel joint and small tailwheel, with fork rods attaching the wheel axle, navy tire, and cream hub, then adjusting the leg's upper attachment point to meet the swivel top cleanly.

Now I'm sizing the wheel itself: a torus for the tire oriented along the X axis so the axle matches the joint direction, with a slightly fattened tube for a cartoonish look, plus a cream cylindrical hubcap and a circular spoke detail centered on the hub.

For the tread, I'm giving the tire a paint function that alternates lug shading around the ring using the torus's circumferential UV coordinate, creating a simple dark/light lug pattern for visual interest when the wheel spins.

Now I'm moving to the cockpit details: padded leather coaming and cream stitched rim on the torus, dark interior floor, a small control stick with a brass ball top near the pilot seat, and simple hidden instrument panel details tucked between the windscreens that won't be visible from most angles. I'm starting to lay out the pilot figure itself in the rear cockpit position.

Working out the pilot's torso as a brown leather jacket capsule with a lighter collar, two arm capsules running from the shoulders down to gloved hands gripping the control stick, and a scarf torus at the neck.

Now I'm shaping the head: a skin-toned sphere mounted on the pilot joint, with small ear spheres, a nose bump, goggles, a mustache made of curled capsules, and a face decal to add color detail.

I'm also building a leather flight cap as a partial dome over the head, adding flattened earflap spheres on each side, and positioning goggle straps that sit pushed up on the cap.

I'm checking the strap radius fits the cap at that height, matching around 0.215. Then I'm working out where the cap's bottom edge falls relative to the face's eye line, since the SVG eyes sit at head center while goggles rest higher on the forehead, so I need the cap's angular coverage to stop above the brow.

The decal sits at head position (0, 2.54, -0.3), and since the cap overlaps the top of that region, it'll just hide that portion of the decal on the sphere surface, which is fine—I'll position the face features lower within the decal area to stay clear of the cap.

Now I'm working out the layout: the decal height is 0.22 centered at y=2.52, with eyes positioned at the vertical middle and a smiling mouth a bit lower. For the face itself I'm sketching an SVG with black oval eyes with white glints, rosy pink cheeks, a big grinning arc with teeth, and a bushy brown mustache, leaving the nose to be handled by the 3D sphere.

Next I'm setting up a passenger bear in the front cockpit—brown spherical body with a lighter belly patch, figuring out how it should face forward toward the front of the vehicle.

For the bear's head I'm placing a sphere with rounded ears (pink inside), a tan muzzle, dark nose, and small black eye spheres with glints. I'm debating accessories—maybe goggles on the forehead instead of a cap, plus a fluttering red scarf or bow tie, and giving the bear raised arms made of capsules to look like it's cheering, with paw spheres at the ends.

Now I'm planning the body placement so it sits hidden inside the basket's rim, and sketching out the decal textures I'll need: a navy/white/red/yellow roundel for the wing, a cream star with red outline for the tail fin, a spoked hub decal, a pilot face decal, and a banner-style fuselage text reading "AIR CIRCUS" assuming a sans font is available.

Writing bunting flag SVG...

I need to work out the rope sweep with a slight droop and dark coloring, then figure out how frames get positioned along the rope path without bone attachments, just passing body-based options for size, lean, and flow direction so the cards hang naturally.

For the flags hanging along the rope between struts, I'm reasoning through the geometry: the rope runs along the z-axis, so the flag's face should point along x (sideways, visible from outside), meaning flow should be [1,0,0] with the width direction naturally falling along z. A lean of 180 flips the card to point downward along the axis, and since the pennant shape is symmetrical, mirroring isn't an issue.

Now I'm computing the rope's sag between the front and rear struts, working out z-heights at each strut position and building a Catmull-Rom curve through three control points to get the droop, then sampling frames along that path at evenly spaced parameters to place each flag card.

I'm also considering adding bunting across the upper wing trailing edges, deciding streamers on struts aren't needed, and keeping the card count modest. For the fuselage decals, I'm positioning banner decals on both flanks, computing the attachment points and directions based on the fuselage's width at different z-stations so the decals sit flush against the curved surface.

I'm placing the attachment point slightly outside the actual surface to account for how the projection likely works, going inward against the direction vector, so it reliably hits the hull rather than missing it. I'm also deciding to skip roundels and numbering on the fuselage sides and cowl, focusing instead on wing-top roundels positioned symmetrically on either side of the centerline.

Now I'm calculating the exact placement for roundels on the top and bottom wing surfaces, accounting for wing thickness and bevel so the decals sit flush just above or below the paint. I'm also sketching out how the struts will be built using angled box frustums between the wings.

I'm tallying the part count to keep well under the 1000-part budget — wings, flaps, wires, and strut fittings all add up but stay manageable, with thin wire sweeps reduced to fewer sides to save geometry. Writing strut fitting code...

For whimsical touches, I'm picking the propeller as painted wood with yellow tips, finalizing the windscreen, and skipping extras like a mascot, parachute pack, or suitcase in favor of simpler story elements — scarf, banner, bunting, pennant, nav lights, and tail wheel.

Now I'm working out the tail details: striped fin, teal elevators, cream stabilizer with red tips, and brace wire rods connecting the fin top and stabilizer tips down toward the fuselage belly, calculating exact coordinates for where each rod attaches.

Checking that the stabilizer at z=-3.3 and y=1.52 properly intersects the fuselage tail radius. Now computing the hinge positions for the elevator flaps and ailerons based on chord and offset values along z.

I'm checking whether the upper wing strut at x=2.3 interferes with the aileron region spanning x=1.7 to 4.0—the strut's top sits right near the aileron hinge line at z=-0.18 to -0.2, so I need to verify whether the strut box actually overlaps the aileron cutout or stays clear of it within the wing center.

Rather than leave the slight overlap, I'm shifting the rear strut attachment forward—moving the upper rear strut to z≈0.02 and lower to z≈-0.08, and adjusting the front struts' z positions too—to keep everything clear of the aileron notch and the rear cockpit coaming. I'm now defining the cabane strut geometry for both front and rear struts on each side of the fuselage.

Checking the lower wing root position against the fuselage flank, then laying out the rigging wires connecting strut tops and bottoms, plus diagonal drag wires crossing between strut positions. I'm also confirming bone assignment for the wing meshes and moving on to building the navigation light glow spheres.

Placing small glowing bulbs near the upper wing tips, red on the right and green on the left, positioned so they peek slightly past the tip edge. I note that glow() needs a flat material rather than paint, and decide to skip strut-top lamps and cowl headlights for now.

Setting up imports and a color palette for the model, then rotating the torus ring 90 degrees about X so it sits flat in the horizontal plane. Writing color palette...

Still defining color palette...

I realize JS's modulo operator can return negative values for negative inputs, which would break my seam detection logic -- I need a proper fract helper that always wraps into the positive range.

Writing shading logic...

Writing cowl paint logic...

Let me map out the outer and inner radius profile along the height axis, defining key points so the shape transitions smoothly from base to top.

For the engine parts, I'm placing a crank barrel cylinder near the rear with steel/dark coloring, and considering whether the front plate disc needs separate paint or stays part of the cylinder.

Now I'm adding a crank ring in brass, then arranging seven radial cylinder heads around the engine face, each rotated to align along the Z axis with finned caps layered on top for detail.

I'm batching geometries by material into merge groups—brass, steel, etc.—so I can combine shapes before adding them to the body, checking that mergeGeometries handles the null case safely. Then I'm scattering small rivet spheres around the cowl's outer radius for added texture.

Now I'm placing additional brass hardware details: rivets along the lip edge, and bolt-head spheres where the wing struts attach to the upper and lower wing surfaces.

I'm skipping extras like seat belts, pitot tubes, placards, and wing-walker rails as unnecessary detail, but I'll add a small brass inspection panel or fuel cap cylinder centered on the top wing. With the ornamentation settled, I'm ready to compile everything together.

Setting up the builder with a 2048 paint size, estimating the texel density needed across the painted surface area (roughly 80 m² of wings and fuselage) to keep rib lines and panel seams crisp, which points toward using a 2048 texture even though it roughly doubles the painted surface resolution requirement.

Now I'm defining the body joint near the center of mass as the root, then building out the wheel joints symmetrically for left and right sides using mirrored positions and directions, adding torus tires, cylindrical hubs colored red, and circular hub cap decals offset along the axle.

I'm checking the geometry fits properly -- tire outer radius matches tube dimensions, torus segment counts give a reasonable triangle budget, and the hub cylinder's radius and depth sit nested inside the tire's inner hole without clipping through the visible sidewall.

Then I'm placing a small brass axle nut sphere at the hub's center, and briefly considering gear legs, axle rods, and mudguards, deciding to skip the mudguards for now.

For the tail wheel, I'm setting up a swivel joint and a hinge joint for the wheel itself, then defining the torus wheel geometry, hub cylinder, and steel fork rods connecting the swivel to the wheel axle on both sides.

Now I'm sketching a windscreen helper function that builds an outline profile from width and height parameters to create the arched canopy shape.

I realize the glass needs to be thicker than the frame instead, so it pokes slightly past the frame on both sides and stays visible as a rim: frame thickness 0.04, glass thickness 0.06, bevel 0.015. Now I'm adjusting the tilt axes for positioning and checking how the y-direction tilt affects the glass outline's height scaling.

I'm now working out the vertical and longitudinal placement of the windscreens relative to the fuselage coaming and the two cockpits. The bear's windscreen sits forward near the coaming front edge so the bear's body is shielded but its head rises above the glass, while the pilot's windscreen sits further back near the rear cockpit coaming — I'm checking that this second windscreen ends up correctly positioned just behind the bear's cockpit rather than overlapping it.

I'm defining the cockpit coaming geometry: a scaled cylinder with leather paint plus a torus rim rotated and scaled so the tube cross-section comes out with the right proportions after the rotation remaps local axes into world space.

Now I'm checking the rim and interior disc positioning against the fuselage surface, calculating the vertical drop at the sides to make sure the coaming bottom edge sits below the fuselage top line at both the front and rear seat positions.

With the geometry confirmed, I'm checking the pilot's torso capsule placement to verify the chest clears the disc and the bottom stays hidden inside the fuselage, then positioning the head above the jacket's top.

Now I'm resolving the small overlap between the head and upper wing by scaling the torso radius down slightly and adjusting the head joint and center heights until there's a comfortable gap under the wing, then setting up a scarf torus around the neck to sit snugly against the head.

Working out the scarf chain path next, dipping and curving it back and downward along the spine so it clears the upper wing, tapering its radius outward along the chain.

For the scarf ribbon, I decide to paint alternating yellow and red stripes using the chain parameter directly, giving it a striped look without needing a separate tassel. Then I move on to defining the bear's head joint position and orientation.
